modules.comments:
The columns engine (0.4): nodes as big as the caller says, in columns
by layer, with ribbons from port to port. Pure, so it runs in node.

WHY A SECOND ENGINE OF ITS OWN, AND NOT THE SANKEY ENGINE TAUGHT PORTS.
The Sankey layout's whole method is that a node is as tall as what
passes through it, and that a node's edges stack along its side by
where they go. A table drawn with its rows is the opposite case on both
counts: it is as tall as its rows, which only the caller knows, and an
edge belongs beside the row it governs, which only the caller knows. A
table does not conserve width either (240 rows in, one total out). So
the Sankey engine keeps its promises and this engine makes others: it
keeps the sizes and ports the picture fixes (`Picture.fixed`), and
draws every edge as a ribbon at one stated scale, with a least breadth
so that a single unit still shows.

WHAT IT DOES.

- **Layers.** The core's `layers` (longest path from a node nothing
  enters), and then a node nothing enters is moved as late as it can go:
  to the layer before the first of the nodes it feeds. A parameter then
  stands beside the table it feeds, not in the first column with every
  other source.
- **Columns.** One column for each layer, as wide as its widest node, the
  columns `layerGap` apart; a node is centred in its column, so the
  nodes of one layer have their middles in one line (`LayersAligned`).
- **Down the page.** Each node is pulled towards the places of the
  nodes at the other ends of its edges, each edge weighing as much as it
  is broad, and measured from where the edge meets the node (its port
  where the port is placed, else the middle of the side): a sweep with
  the flow (by what enters a node) and one against it (by what leaves),
  `passes` times. After each pull a column is put in the order its nodes
  want, pushed apart to `nodeGap`, and moved as a whole by the mean of
  what the push cost, so that it does not creep down the page.
- **No deeper than `deepest`.** A table drawn with every row is some
  thousands of pixels tall, and a small node that feeds its middle is
  pulled level with that middle, a long way under the first screenful.
  Where the spacing says `deepest: Just limit`, no node begins more than
  `limit` under the top of the picture, unless the nodes above it in
  its own column leave it no room: after the pulling, each column is
  taken from the top down, and a node below the limit is raised to it
  or to `nodeGap` under the node above, whichever is lower. The order
  of a column's nodes is kept. The ribbon then runs down to the row it
  governs. `Nothing` (the default) raises nothing.
- **Routes.** A ribbon from where an edge leaves its source to where it
  enters its target: at a placed port where the edge names one the node
  has placed, and otherwise stacked on the node's right side (leaving)
  or left (entering), centred on the side's middle, in the order of the
  other ends down the page. One cubic piece, level at both ends. An
  edge into a layer no later than its source's is turned back
  (`Backward`) and loops out and back by a layer's gap.

WHAT IT PROMISES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. `FlowsForward`, `LayersAligned`,
`KeepsFixed` and `WidthsScaled` at the scaling it is made with. Not
`WidthsConserved`: a node is not as tall as what passes through it.
Not `RoutesOrthogonal`: its routes are curves. It draws no outlines:
told of open groups it outlines none, and the general law `Outlined`
says so. Ribbons that meet one port, or that are stacked at a side,
stand beside one another; ribbons that meet different ports stand
where the caller put the ports, and whether those overlap is the
caller's to say.

declarations.comments:
`layerGap`: between one column and the next. `nodeGap`: between two
nodes of a column. `margin`: round the picture. `nodeWidth`,
`nodeHeight`: the size of a node the picture does not fix (taller
where its words need it). `passes`: how many times the nodes are pulled
down the page, each time with the flow and against it. `deepest`: how
far under the top of the picture a node may begin, where its column
has room (the header says how); `Nothing` for as far as it is pulled.
declarations.title: Spacing

declarations.comments: The columns engine at a spacing and a scaling of widths.
declarations.title: columns

modules.comments:
What is kept between two layouts of two cuts of one flow, measured
(0.6).

When a group opens or closes, the reader must not lose their place.
There is a ladder of what a pair of pictures can promise, best first;
this module computes the three rungs that are laws of the pair, from
the two layouts and nothing else, so that a page says which rung it is
on and adds other signals accordingly. It claims a rung only where it
has measured it.

- `Held`: every node the change does not touch keeps its box exactly,
  and the pair is `Nested`.
- `Nested`: each opened group's parts lie within the breadth its
  closed bar had, where the bar stood: every part's span across the
  flow is inside the bar's span. And the pair is `Ordered`.
- `Ordered`: things move, but no two nodes of a tier and no two
  ribbons at a node change order.
- `Rearranged`: none of these. (The ladder's other rungs, a watched
  transition and signals in colour and outline, are then all the
  reader has.)

HOW A CHANGE IS READ FROM TWO LAYOUTS. A node is *untouched* when its
key is in both. A *bar* is a closed group's node (its step, or its
summary) that is in one layout and not the other; its *parts* are the
members of that group's outline in the other layout, which is why the
layouts must have been made with the picture told of its groups. A
node in one layout only that is neither a bar with parts nor a part of
a bar is *unaccounted for*, and a pair with such a node is not called
`Nested`. Nothing here is told which layout is the finer: several
groups may open and others close between the two, and each bar is
paired with its parts wherever they are.

ORDER, exactly. Two untouched nodes in one tier of both layouts are
across the flow from one another the same way in both. A bar is to an
untouched node of its tier as each of its parts is to that node, where
they share a tier. On each side of an untouched node, the ribbons to
(or from) two different other ends stand the same way in both, a
ribbon to a part counting as a ribbon to its bar; and so the ribbons
to the parts of one group stand together. Two things at one place (a
node of no breadth, a ribbon of none) are in order either way. Nodes
with no tier (the shelf) are not compared.

declarations.comments: The best rung a pair keeps; see the module's header.
declarations.title: Continuity

declarations.comments:
A closed group's bar in one layout and its parts in the other.
`breadth`: the bar's, across the flow. `slot`: from the start of the
first part to the end of the last, in any tier (so the parts fit a
slot of the bar's breadth when `slot <= breadth`). `abreast`: the most
the parts of one tier come to, added up. `inPlace`: every part's span
is inside the span the bar had.
declarations.title: Bar

declarations.comments:
Everything measured of a pair. `moved`: the untouched nodes whose box
is not what it was. `unaccounted`: see the header. `disordered`: each
breach of order, in words.
declarations.title: Change

declarations.comments: A closed group's bar in one layout, and its parts in another.
declarations.title: Opened

declarations.comments:
The bars of the first layout that the second has not, each with its
parts in the second: the members there of its group's outline. (A bar
whose group has no outline in the second layout is not among them.)
declarations.title: opened

declarations.comments: What is kept between two layouts, and what is not.
declarations.title: change

declarations.comments: The best rung two layouts of two cuts of one flow keep.
declarations.title: continuity

modules.comments:
What any layout engine makes, and an engine as a value.

In 0.2 the renderer had one layout, the Sankey layout, and its types
were that layout's: a `Layout` was what `layout` returned, a picture
held Sankey `Metrics` and `Widths`, and the laws asserted Sankey facts.
A trial that drew the same flows with a second engine had to pass its result off as a Sankey layout. This module
is the layout result with the Sankey layout taken out of it, so that the
tree draws a `Layout` and the laws and measures read one without
knowing which engine made it.

It is designed for three engines and no others: the Sankey layout
(`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Sankey`), `layered-layout` (ports, right-angled
routes, no widths; its adapter lives outside this package,
which must not depend on it), and Stemma, a rewrite of Graphviz dot
(clusters, splines, ranks, top-down by default).

THE DECISIONS, each with its reason.

- **A route is data** (`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Route`), and a placed
  edge has no `path`, `start`, `end`, `width` or `stroke` of its own:
  each is read from the route (`Route.svgPath`, `Route.start`, …), so
  none can disagree with it.
- **Ports are placed on nodes** (`PlacedNode.ports`). A placed port is
  which port (its name, and whether it is one of the node's inputs or
  its outputs: a step may have an input and an output of one name), the
  side of the box it is on, and how far along that side: so it is on
  the box's boundary by construction, and `portPoint` says where. An
  engine places the ports it gives a place to and no others: the Sankey
  layout stacks a node's edges by where they go, not by port, and
  places none. Whether an edge meets a port is not a field of the edge:
  the edge already names its ports (`Edge.fromPort`, `Edge.toPort`, the
  core's), and the law is that where the node has that port placed the
  route ends there.
- **`direction` is the layout's**, not the tree's or the caller's: the
  engine knows which way it ran. The laws read "forward" and "aligned"
  by it, and the tree sets a node's words by it.
- **`layer` stays a `Maybe`.** It is the layer (dot's rank) the engine
  put a node in *of the whole picture*, and some placed nodes have
  none: the Sankey layout's shelf of nodes no edge touches, and every
  node of a layout made of several layerings (`layered-layout` run once
  for each open group). Both are real, so the case is not designed
  out; what is designed out is a layer that means something only
  within a part of the picture.
- **An engine is a value** (`Engine`): a name, the function, and what
  it promises. A `Picture` is what every engine is told beside the
  projection: what is written in a node, and which groups are open.
  What only one engine can be told (the Sankey layout's `Metrics` and
  `Widths`, the other's spacings) is that engine's own configuration,
  given where the engine is made (`sankey metrics widths`), and is not
  in `Picture`. Node breadth is among those: an engine may size a node
  as it likes, and the law about words reads the breadth a node was
  given from its own box.
- **Promises are a closed ADT** (`Promise`), one constructor for each
  law that holds of some engines and not of all. A promise carries what
  its law needs and no layout holds: `WidthsConserved` carries the scale
  and the edge's quantity. `Hylograph.Flow.Render.Laws` checks the
  general laws of every layout and, of an engine's layout, exactly the
  laws it promises: an engine that does not conserve widths is not
  asked to, so nothing has to be suppressed.
- **A caller may fix a node** (`Picture.fixed`, since 0.4): its size,
  and where its ports are. Until 0.4 an engine sized every node itself
  (from its words, or from what its edges carry), which is right for a
  box and a name and wrong for a node whose inside the caller draws
  (a table of rows: only the caller knows how tall it is, and how far
  down its side each row stands). A fixed node is a size and placed
  ports, the same `PlacedPort` an engine makes, so the general law that
  a route meets a placed port needs nothing new to hold the engine to
  the caller's places. Keeping the fix is a promise (`KeepsFixed`) and
  not a general law: an engine whose node sizes are its whole method
  (the Sankey layout's, which are the widths) cannot keep it, and is
  not asked to.

declarations.comments:
Which way the flow runs in a layout: its layers are columns
(`LeftToRight`) or rows (`TopDown`).
declarations.title: Direction

declarations.comments: A side of a box.

A port with a place. `along`: how far along `side` it is, in pixels
from the side's top (a left or right side) or its left end (a top or
bottom side).

declarations.comments: Where on the picture a port of a box is.
declarations.title: portPoint

declarations.comments:
`Forward`: with the flow. `Backward`: an edge the engine turned back to
close a cycle (a scan reading what it wrote).
declarations.title: Course

declarations.comments:
`index`: the node's place in the projection. `layer`: its layer in the
whole picture, where the engine gave it one (see the module's header).
`words`: what is written in it, as set, where the picture said
(`Picture.words`); `Nothing` where it did not. `ports`: the ports the
engine gave a place; none for an item, which has none.

`index`: the edge's place in the projection. `edge`: the projection's
own, with the wires it stands for, so what is known of a wire can be
shown on it. `route`: the line it is drawn along, from its source to
its target.

declarations.comments:
An open group's outline. Since 0.7 a group may have more than one: see
`runsOf`. `name`: the group's, from the grouping.
`header`: the height of the strip at the top of `box` that is kept for
the name. `depth`: how many outlines it is inside; `parent`: the
nearest. `members`: the indices of the nodes inside it, however deep.
declarations.title: PlacedOutline

declarations.comments:
The outlines of a layout, each with which of its group's it is: 0 for
the first in the layout's order, 1 for the next of the same group, and
so on (0.7). An engine that draws a group whose members stand in
separate runs of tiers as tied outlines (the unfolding engine) gives
the group one outline for each run, in order along the flow; every
other engine gives each group one, and every run is 0.
declarations.title: runsOf

declarations.comments: A group's outline for one of its runs, if it has that many.
declarations.title: runAt

declarations.comments:
What a part of a closed group does at the group's boundary, where it
does only one thing: it only receives (a dead end), or only gives (a
spring).
declarations.title: Only

declarations.comments:
A closed group's bar with its seams (0.7): the parts the group opens
into, where they stand side by side and together are exactly as broad
as the bar. `node`: the bar's index in the layout. Each part is from
`from` to `to` across the flow, measured from the bar's start; `only`
is said where the bar itself both receives and gives and the part does
one of them alone.
declarations.title: Seamed

declarations.comments:
Nodes and edges in the projection's order. An edge with an end that is
no node of the projection has no place and is left out (`project` makes
none). Outlines outermost first, so drawn in order an outline is over
the one that holds it; none unless the picture told of groups.
declarations.title: Layout

declarations.comments:
The grouping, and the groups that are closed: what `collapse` was given
to make the flow that was projected. Every other group is open.
declarations.title: Groups

declarations.comments:
`padding`: from an outline to what is in it. `header`: the strip for
the group's name.
declarations.title: OutlineMetrics

declarations.comments:
What a caller fixes of a node: how big its box is, and where its ports
are (each on a side of that box, as an engine would place it). A port
not listed is left to the engine; a node fixed with no ports has its
size fixed and nothing else.
declarations.title: FixedNode

declarations.comments:
What every engine is told beside the projection. `words`: what is
written in each node, for the engine to wrap to the breadth it gives
the node and make room for; `Nothing` leaves every node as tall as the
engine makes it and its label to the tree, on one line. `groups`: the
open groups to outline; `Nothing` for none. `fixed`: the nodes whose
size and ports the caller fixes, for an engine that promises to keep
them (`KeepsFixed`); `const Nothing` fixes none.
declarations.title: Picture

declarations.comments: No words set, no group outlined, no node fixed.
declarations.title: plainPicture

declarations.comments:
The open groups a drawn element is in, outermost first, and every
group's name. A step is where `Member` puts it and an item where
`Holds` does; a closed group's step and its summary are in the groups
their group is in; an item a closed group holds that is drawn all the
same (an open step writes it) is in the open groups over that group.
An element no group holds is in none.
declarations.title: openPaths

declarations.comments:
What the law of conserved widths needs and no layout holds: the pixels
to one unit of width, and an edge's width in units.
declarations.title: Conservation

declarations.comments:
What the law of scaled widths needs: the pixels to one unit of width,
the least breadth a ribbon is drawn at (so that one unit still shows),
and an edge's width in units.
declarations.title: Scaling

declarations.comments:
How broad a ribbon of so many units is at a scaling: its units at the
scale, and never less than the least. Units that are not a positive
number are none, and drawn at the least.
declarations.title: scaledBreadth

declarations.comments:
A law that holds of some engines' layouts and not of every layout; an
engine lists the ones it keeps. What each says exactly is in
`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Laws`.

- `FlowsForward`: an edge not turned back runs with the flow, and where
  the projection has no cycle no edge is turned back.
- `LayersAligned`: the nodes of one layer stand in one line across the
  flow.
- `RoutesOrthogonal`: every route is straight legs along the axes.
- `WidthsConserved`: every route is a ribbon as broad as its quantity
  says, and at each node the ribbons of a side stand in the node, beside
  one another, and the node is as tall as the broader side.
- `KeepsFixed` (0.4): every node the picture fixes has the size it was
  given and exactly the ports it was given, where it was given them.
- `WidthsScaled` (0.4): every route is a ribbon as broad as its units
  at the scale, or the least breadth where that is more. Nothing is
  said of the node: an engine that keeps the caller's sizes cannot also
  make a node as tall as what passes through it (a table of 240 rows
  gives one value: 240 units in, one out).
- `WidthsCarried` (0.6): as `WidthsConserved`, but a node is *at least*
  as broad as its broader side, not exactly: the unfolding engine's
  closed group is as broad as the most of its inside that is ever
  abreast, which can be more than crosses its boundary.
- `StaysWithin` (0.7): the ink of every route is inside the picture,
  a ribbon turned back and broad among them.
declarations.title: Promise

declarations.comments:
A layout engine: what it is called, what it promises of every layout it
makes, and the making.
declarations.title: Engine

declarations.comments: An engine's layout of a projection.

modules.name: Hylograph.Flow.Render.Engine

modules.comments:
Room made down the page: for nodes taller than their edges make them,
and for the outlines of open groups.

The Sankey layout gives every box (a node, or the waypoint of a long
edge) a column and a place down it, with one gap between any two boxes
of a column. It has no way to be told that this box needs to be taller,
or that these boxes are to stand in a frame that nothing else enters.
This module moves boxes down, and only down, until both hold.

What it is given is a forest of *blocks* in the order they are to stand
in, top to bottom: a block is one box, or a cluster of blocks (an open
group). A block's *extent* is the columns it spans, first to last, and
its top and bottom; a cluster's is the extent of what is in it, with
`padding` all round and `header` more above. The blocks of one level
are taken in order, and each is moved down, rigidly, by the least that
puts its top `gap` under the bottom of every earlier block of its level
in **every column of its extent**, whether or not it has a box in that
column. So the extents of the blocks of a level are disjoint
rectangles (in columns by top and bottom), which is what makes an
outline hold its members and nothing else.

That works only when the order given agrees, in every column, with the
order the boxes already stand in (a block never moves up past another).
The caller sees to that: it holds the Sankey layout to the same order
with `nodeSort`.

A box with no place yet (`top: Nothing`: a member of an open group that
no edge touches, which the Sankey layout would put on a shelf far from
its group) is stood under what its level already has in its column.

declarations.comments:
One box. `top`: where the Sankey layout put it; `Nothing` for a box it
did not place. `height`: how tall it is to be.
declarations.title: Leaf

declarations.comments:
`gap`: between two blocks of a level. `padding`: from a cluster's
contents to its frame. `header`: more room above, for the group's name.
declarations.title: Spacing

declarations.comments:
A cluster as placed. `depth`: how many clusters it is inside.
`levels`: how many levels of cluster are inside it. `leaves`: every box
in it, however deep.
declarations.title: Frame

declarations.comments:
`tops`: each box's top, by name. `frames`: outermost first. `bottom`:
the lowest bottom of anything (0 where there is nothing).
declarations.title: Arranged

declarations.comments: The names of every box of a block.
declarations.title: leavesOf

modules.name: Hylograph.Flow.Render.Internal.Bands

modules.comments:
The keyboard, for a drawn flow (0.5).

The tree tells a caller of clicks and of the pointer (`Decoration.notify`)
through HATS, which has no behaviour for a key. A mark the decoration
calls a button (`Decoration.button`) can be focused; `pressByKeys` is
the other half: one listener on a container, under which Enter or Space
on a focused button of a drawn flow is a click on that button, told as
any click is. It is attached once, to an element that outlives
redrawing (the container the tree is rendered into), and not to the
marks, which come and go.

This is the package's one foreign module and it needs a document, so
nothing here runs in node; the pure half (which marks are buttons, and
what each says) is in `Tree` and is tested there.

declarations.comments:
Under every element the selector finds, make Enter and Space on a
focused button of a drawn flow a click on it. Returns how to stop.
declarations.title: pressByKeys

modules.name: Hylograph.Flow.Render.Keys

modules.comments:
What must hold of a layout, as functions that return what does not.
Here, and not in a test directory, so that every adapter's tests can
hold the layout of its own real flows to it, and every engine's author
can hold the engine to it.

THE LAWS ARE SPLIT BY WHAT THEY ARE TRUE OF. In 0.2 there was one list,
and it was the Sankey layout's: an edge as wide as its quantity says, a
node as tall as its wider side. A correct layout by another engine was
reported as dozens of faults. Now:

**General laws** hold of any layout of any projection under any
picture, whichever engine made it (`generalFaults`):

- `Placed`: each node of the projection has exactly one place, in the
  projection's order, and each edge one;
- `Finite`: every number is finite (boxes, ports, routes, outlines, the
  picture's size) and no box has a negative side;
- `Within`: every node's box and every outline is inside the picture;
- `Apart`: no two node boxes overlap;
- `Ported`: a placed port is one of its node's own (an input of that
  name, or an output), is placed once, and is within its side's length;
- `Routed`: every route starts on the box of the node its edge is from
  and ends on the box of the node it is to (on the boundary, to within
  `meeting`), and where the edge names a port and the node has that
  port placed, at the port; and a polyline's jumps are on the polyline;
- `Lettered`: where the picture sets words, every node has its words
  set, within the lines allowed; no line is wider than the node's own
  breadth has room for, as the estimate has it (a single character too
  wide for the room aside); and the node is tall enough for them. Where
  it sets none, no node has any;
- `Outlined`: there is an outline for each open group that holds a
  node, and none where the picture tells of no group; its members are
  the nodes the grouping puts in it, however deep; every member is
  inside its outline, under the strip for its name; an outline's parent
  is the nearest open group over it, and the outline is inside its
  parent's, under the parent's strip; the outlines of two groups
  overlap only where one holds the other; and no node that is not a
  member is in an outline, or partly in it. **A group may have several
  outlines (0.7)**, one for each run of its members where they stand in
  separate runs of tiers (the unfolding engine's tied outlines): then
  each member is in exactly one of them, they do not overlap one
  another, and each is inside one of its parent's. Until 0.7 the law
  asked for exactly one, which no layout of one outline to a group
  breaks now.

**Promised laws** hold of the layouts of an engine that promises them
(`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Engine.Promise`), and are asked of no other
(`promiseFaults`):

- `FlowForward` (`FlowsForward`): an edge not turned back ends further
  along the flow than it starts (to the right, or below, by the
  layout's direction), and in a later layer where both its nodes have
  one; and where the projection has no cycle no edge is turned back;
- `LayerAlignment` (`LayersAligned`): the nodes of one layer have their
  middles in one line across the flow, and a later layer's line is
  further along it;
- `Orthogonality` (`RoutesOrthogonal`): every route is a polyline, each
  leg of which runs along an axis;
- `Conservation` (`WidthsConserved`): every route is a ribbon, as broad
  as its width says at the promise's scale; the ribbons on one side of
  a node stand inside the node and beside one another; and the node is
  as tall as the broader side, or as its words need where that is more.
  (Checked where every width is positive.)
- `FixedKept` (`KeepsFixed`, 0.4): every node the picture fixes has
  the width and height it was given, and its placed ports are exactly
  the ports it was given, each on the side and as far along it as it
  was given. (That a route meets each of them is the general law
  `Routed`, already.)
- `Scaled` (`WidthsScaled`, 0.4): every route is a ribbon whose breadth
  is its units at the promise's scale, or the promise's least breadth
  where that is more (`Engine.scaledBreadth`). Unlike `Conservation` it
  says nothing of how tall a node is, or of how ribbons stand at a
  node: the engines that promise it keep the caller's sizes and ports,
  and how ribbons stand at a port is then the caller's to arrange.

- `Carried` (`WidthsCarried`, 0.6): as `Conservation`, but the node is
  at least as broad as its broader side, not exactly.
- `InkWithin` (`StaysWithin`, 0.7): the ink of every route is inside
  the picture: a ribbon as broad as it is drawn, flat across the flow
  where it goes forward as a band and square to its line otherwise
  (`Measures.inkOf`), to within half a pixel. The general law `Within`
  says nothing of routes, which is how a broad ribbon turned back,
  stroked round a turn tighter than its own breadth, ran off the
  picture unreported until 0.7. It is a promise and not part of
  `Within` because the Sankey engine does not keep it (its turns are
  of one size whatever the ribbon's breadth), and its layouts are not
  changed here.

`check engine picture projection layout` is the general laws and

modules.comments:
The door 0.2 came in by: `layout metrics widths projection`, which is
the Sankey engine run on a picture with no words and no groups, and the
names 0.2 imported from here.

Since 0.3 the layout is pluggable, and this module holds none of it:

- `Hylograph.Flow.Render.Engine` is what any engine makes (`Layout`,
  placed nodes with their ports, placed edges with their routes,
  outlines, the direction), what every engine is told (`Picture`), and
  an engine as a value (`Engine`, `Promise`, `run`);
- `Hylograph.Flow.Render.Route` is an edge's route as data;
- `Hylograph.Flow.Render.Sankey` is the Sankey engine, with `Metrics`
  and `Widths` as its own configuration.

Everything here is one of theirs under the name it had, so that code
written for 0.2 that calls `layout` and reads boxes still compiles. For
words, open groups or another engine: `run engine picture projection`.

The Sankey engine's layout of a projection with no words set and no
group outlined: `run (sankey metrics widths) plainPicture`.

declarations.comments: A side of a box.

declarations.comments:
A law that holds of some engines' layouts and not of every layout; an
engine lists the ones it keeps. What each says exactly is in
`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Laws`.

- `FlowsForward`: an edge not turned back runs with the flow, and where
  the projection has no cycle no edge is turned back.
- `LayersAligned`: the nodes of one layer stand in one line across the
  flow.
- `RoutesOrthogonal`: every route is straight legs along the axes.
- `WidthsConserved`: every route is a ribbon as broad as its quantity
  says, and at each node the ribbons of a side stand in the node, beside
  one another, and the node is as tall as the broader side.
- `KeepsFixed` (0.4): every node the picture fixes has the size it was
  given and exactly the ports it was given, where it was given them.
- `WidthsScaled` (0.4): every route is a ribbon as broad as its units
  at the scale, or the least breadth where that is more. Nothing is
  said of the node: an engine that keeps the caller's sizes cannot also
  make a node as tall as what passes through it (a table of 240 rows
  gives one value: 240 units in, one out).
- `WidthsCarried` (0.6): as `WidthsConserved`, but a node is *at least*
  as broad as its broader side, not exactly: the unfolding engine's
  closed group is as broad as the most of its inside that is ever
  abreast, which can be more than crosses its boundary.
- `StaysWithin` (0.7): the ink of every route is inside the picture,
  a ribbon turned back and broad among them.

A port with a place. `along`: how far along `side` it is, in pixels

`header`: the height of the strip at the top of `box` that is kept for
the name. `depth`: how many outlines it is inside; `parent`: the
nearest. `members`: the indices of the nodes inside it, however deep.
declarations.title: PlacedOutline

declarations.comments:
`index`: the node's place in the projection. `layer`: its layer in the

`words`: what is written in it, as set, where the picture said

engine gave a place; none for an item, which has none.

`index`: the edge's place in the projection. `edge`: the projection's

What every engine is told beside the projection. `words`: what is

modules.comments:
Measures of a drawn graph, whoever laid it out: the scoreboard of an
earlier layout trial, here so that every engine is scored by one rule.

Every measure is a function of a `Drawn` and nothing else: node boxes,
each edge as the straight pieces it is drawn along, and the boxes of
the open groups' outlines with their members. `drawnOf` makes a `Drawn`
of any `Layout`, each route by `Hylograph.Flow.Render.Route.flatten`: a
straight piece is its two ends, a cubic curve is `curveSteps` (12)
straight pieces. So a ribbon, a dog-leg and a spline are measured by
one rule, and no engine's own counts are used. A `Drawn` can also be
made by hand, which is how the measures are held to figures worked out
on paper. (The trial read each edge back from its SVG path; the pieces
are the same, so its figures stand.)

THE MEASURES, exactly, as the trial stated them.

- `crossings`: the number of points at which a piece of one edge's
  line properly crosses a piece of another edge's: each piece's two
  ends strictly on opposite sides of the other piece. Touching does not
  count: two edges that leave one point, an edge that turns exactly on
  another, and two edges that run along one line (a shared trunk) cross
  nowhere. Two edges that cross twice count twice. **Nor does meeting
  at a shared end**: where the two edges have a node in common and the
  point of crossing is within `skin` (1 pixel) of where each of them
  ends at that node, they meet there, as two edges into one port do
  when their ends are computed a hair apart; any other crossing of two
  edges with a node in common counts. (Since 0.3.1; before, such a
  meeting counted one.) **A crossing at a point where a line is cut
  into pieces counts too (0.7)**: where one line has a corner on the
  other (on a corner of it, or within one of its pieces) and the two
  pieces either side of that corner lie strictly on opposite sides of
  the other line there, the lines cross once. Until 0.7 that was a
  touch and scored nothing, which missed the commonest crossing a
  layered layout has: two neighbours of a tier that change places on
  the way to the next cross exactly at the middle of their two curves,
  and the middle is where a curve is cut. A corner that touches and
  turns back, and two lines that share a stretch, still cross nowhere.
- `edgeLength`: the sum of the lengths of every edge's line, pixels.
- `bends`: total turning, in right angles: the sum over every interior
  point of every line of the angle turned there, divided by 90
  degrees. An orthogonal route scores one for each corner; a curve
  scores by how far it swings (an S that reaches 45 degrees and comes
  back scores one), and a straight line nothing.
- `extent`: the box round every node, outline and edge point; `area` is
  its width times its height, in pixels squared, and `aspect` its width
  over its height.
- `nodeOverlaps`: the pairs of node boxes with more than a touch in
  common (more than `skin`, 1 pixel, each way).
- `edgesThroughNodes`: the pairs of an edge and a node that is neither
  of its ends, where the edge's line enters the node's box drawn in by
  `skin` on every side.
- `outlineTrespasses`: the pairs of an edge and an outline where neither
  end of the edge is a member of the outline's group and the edge's
  line enters the outline's box drawn in by `skin`. (An edge with an
  end inside must cross the outline, and is not counted.)
- `strangersIn`: the pairs of an outline and a node that is no member
  of it and is in its box or partly in it: the general law
  (`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Laws.strangers`), counted.
- `unrouted`: the edges with no line (fewer than two points). No route
  of a `Layout` is such (`Route` cannot be), so of a layout this is 0
  unless a route's points are all one point; it is here for a `Drawn`
  made otherwise. An edge an engine left out altogether is the laws'
  to report (`Placed`), and `unplaced` counts them.

Time to lay out is not here: it is measured by whoever runs the layout.

THE MEASURES OF LEGIBILITY (0.7). The measures above score a drawing as
a graph. These score it as something a general reader has to follow,
by four heuristics that are **guesses** (Andrew's word) and are here to
be calibrated; the numbers they are held against are `thresholds`, in
this one place. They need what a `Drawn` has not: how broad each ribbon
is, what colour it is drawn in, and which way the flow runs. That is a
`Banded` (`bandedOf` makes one of a layout and a colour for each edge;
it can be made by hand).

- `overlaps`: the pairs of ribbons that cross (their middle lines, by
  `crossings`' rule) or overlie one another (their ink has more than
  `thresholds.overlap` square pixels in common), each with that area.
  `overlapsInOneColour` are those drawn in one colour: the ones a
  reader cannot follow through. The area is exact where both ribbons
  are swept bands (flat across the flow: a forward ribbon as the tree's
  `Swept` draws it); a ribbon drawn as a stroke (turned back, or a
  hairline) is taken piece by piece and its corners counted twice, so
  its areas are a little over.
- `proportions`: of each ribbon, its run along the flow, its breadth
  (the data's, not the ink's), and how far it travels across the flow;
  `squat` are those whose run is less than `thresholds.proportion`
  times its breadth, or times its travel.
- `pictureProportion`: the picture's length along the flow over its
  breadth across it.
- `againstTheFlow`: the ribbons that anywhere run backward along the
  flow by more than `thresholds.against` pixels in all, read from
  their lines and not from what the engine says of them.

A layout as drawn: its node boxes in the layout's order, its edges as

The pairs of an outline and a node that is no member of it and is in

declarations.comments:
How far inside a box an edge must come to be in it, and how much two
boxes must share to overlap: 1 pixel.

declarations.comments:
What the measures of legibility are held against, and what the engines
and the tree take from them. Guesses, to be calibrated.

- `proportion`: a ribbon, and a picture, should be at least this many
  times as long along the flow as it is broad across it (and a ribbon
  that many times as long as it travels across).
- `overlap`: two ribbons overlie one another when their ink has more
  than this in common, in square pixels.
- `against`: a ribbon runs against the flow when it runs backward by
  more than this, in pixels.
- `hair`: a ribbon less broad than this, in pixels, cannot be seen; the
  unfolding engine draws it this broad and says it is not to scale.
- `nameReach`: an open group's name should be within this of where its
  closed bar's name was, in pixels.

A ribbon as it is drawn. `edge`: its index in the layout. `from`,
`to`: the places of its two nodes among the layout's nodes (-1 where it
has none). `breadth`: the data's. `ink`: how broad it is drawn.
`swept`: drawn flat across the flow (a band going forward), not as a
stroke along its line.

going forward is taken as swept, as the unfolding pages draw it
(`Tree.Swept`); a route that is no ribbon is a line 1.25 broad
(`Tree.hairline`).

The same, by its public name: the corners of a ribbon's ink, piece by
piece, for a law that the ink is inside the picture.

edges' indices, the lesser first. `area`: the ink they have in common.
`crossings`: how many times their middle lines cross.

A ribbon's shape. `run`: how far its line reaches along the flow.
`travel`: how far it reaches across it. `byBreadth`, `byTravel`: the
run over each (as great as can be where there is none of it).

modules.name: Hylograph.Flow.Render.Measures

modules.comments:
Whether the reader has asked for less motion (0.6): the browser's
`prefers-reduced-motion`. A page that watches a change of cut
(`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Transition`) asks this first, and where the
answer is yes makes the change at once and signals it another way
(`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Signal`). Needs a window, so it does not run
in node; with none it answers no.
modules.name: Hylograph.Flow.Render.Motion

modules.comments:
Present mode: nothing hidden, the folded parts drawn quiet (0.6).

An alternative to folding. The picture is the layout with every group
open, whatever the cut; the groups the cut closes are *quiet*: their
nodes are still there, at their breadths, with their ribbons, and are
made to take less of the eye.

THE RULE IN A SANKEY: BREADTH IS DATA AND IS NEVER REDUCED. A quiet
node may lose length along the flow, its colour, and its words; it may
not get narrower, and neither may a ribbon. So de-emphasis is two
things and no others: `present` shortens a quiet node along the flow
(about its middle, its ribbons following its sides), and `quietly`
marks quiet nodes and the ribbons between two of them with the class
`flow-quiet`, for a stylesheet to mute. Every node is as broad across
the flow, and every ribbon as broad, as in the layout it was given.

What it does not do: draw the tiers of a quiet group nearer together.
That would move everything downstream of it, which the layout engine
would have to be told of; here only the nodes are shortened.

declarations.comments:
The nodes of a layout that are in a quiet group: the members of those
groups' outlines. (The layout must have been made with the picture told
of its groups, and with them open.)
declarations.title: quietKeys
present

declarations.comments:
A decoration with `flow-quiet` added to the class of every quiet node
and of every edge between two quiet nodes.
declarations.title: quietly

declarations.comments: The class a quiet mark is given.
declarations.title: quietClass

modules.name: Hylograph.Flow.Render.Present

modules.comments:
A layout with its boxes moved, its ribbons following; and two layouts
of one projection blended (0.6).

Both are for showing a layout on the way to being another: a transition
between two cuts (`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Transition`), and a node drawn
quiet (`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Present`). Neither places anything: the
boxes are the caller's, and a route goes with its two ends.

WHAT IS KEPT. A route's start goes with the side of its source that it
leaves by and its end with the side of its target that it enters by
(the far side and the near side along the flow), each by exactly as
much as that side moved; what is between goes by as much as its place
along the route says, from the one to the other. So a ribbon stands
where it stood on each node's side, as broad as it was: if widths were
carried before (`Laws.Carried`), they are carried after, exactly, and
every route still meets its nodes (`Laws.Routed`). A route keeps its
pieces, so the layout before and the layout after can be blended piece
by piece. What is not kept: boxes may overlap, a ribbon may cross a
node, and an outline is wherever the caller put it. These are pictures
of a layout in motion, not layouts an engine would make.

declarations.comments:
Where each node's box is to be, and each outline's; and how large the
picture then is.
declarations.title: Reshaping

declarations.comments:
A layout with every box where the reshaping puts it and every route
gone with its ends; see the module's header.
declarations.title: reshaped

declarations.comments:
A layout part of the way from one to another of the same shape
(`sameShape`): every number of the first gone that part of the way to
the second's (0 is the first, 1 the second). A route whose pieces are
not the other's is the first's until half way and the second's after;
an outline that only one of them has is drawn while that one is nearer.
Where both carry widths and their ribbons stand alike on their nodes,
so does every blend of them: a ribbon's end goes with its node's side.
declarations.title: blend

declarations.comments:
Whether two layouts are of one projection, piece for piece: the same
nodes in order, the same edges, and every route of the same pieces. Two
such layouts can be blended.
declarations.title: sameShape

modules.name: Hylograph.Flow.Render.Reshape

modules.comments:
The line an edge is drawn along, as data.

In 0.2 a placed edge held an SVG path string. A string can be drawn and
nothing else: to measure an edge an earlier layout trial had to
parse the string back, and a second layout engine had to print its
routes as strings only for them to be read again. Here the route is a
value, the string is derived from it (`svgPath`), and so are the points
it is measured along (`flatten`).

THE THREE ROUTES. `Route` is closed, and has exactly the routes of the
three engines this renderer is built to take. None is there for an
engine nobody has.

- `Ribbon`, the Sankey layout's: a centre line of straight and cubic
  pieces, and a `breadth`, the room the edge takes on the side of each
  node it touches (its two attachment spans are the centre line's two
  ends, half the breadth either way across the flow). The Sankey
  layout's ribbons are as broad at one end as at the other, so the width
  profile is one number; an engine that tapers one would need a profile
  here, and none of the three does. `ink` says how the ribbon is drawn:
  a `Band` as broad as it is, or a `Hairline` down its middle. It is an
  ADT and not a second number because a stroke beside a breadth is two
  numbers that can disagree, and in a band they are one.
- `Polyline`, `layered-layout`'s: straight legs from point to point,
  and its line jumps (where it hops over an edge it crosses). That the
  bends are right angles is not in the type: that engine's routes
  through nested groups are joined at the group's boundary and may
  slant by a pixel or two there, so right angles are a promise an engine
  makes and a law checks (`RoutesOrthogonal`), not a constructor.
- `Spline`, Graphviz dot's (Stemma): cubic Bézier pieces end to end.

NO ROUTE WITHOUT A LINE. Each constructor has a first point and at least
one more (a `NonEmptyArray` of pieces, or a `to`), so an edge that is
placed has somewhere to be drawn; an engine that cannot route an edge
leaves the edge out, and the law that every edge is placed says so. The
trial's `unrouted` measure counted polylines of fewer than two points;
there is no such value now.

MEASURING. `flatten` is the one rule by which every route becomes
straight pieces: a straight piece is its two ends, a cubic piece is
`curveSteps` (12) straight pieces, and a cubic whose four points lie on
one line is one. It is the trial's rule (it read the same pieces back
from the path string), kept so that its figures stand. A polyline's
jumps are ink, not geometry: they are drawn and not measured.

declarations.comments:
A cubic Bézier piece from where the line has got to: it leaves towards
`leaving`, arrives from `arriving`, and ends at `to`.
declarations.title: Curve

declarations.comments: One piece of a ribbon's centre line, from where the last piece ended.
declarations.title: Piece

declarations.comments:
How a ribbon is drawn: as broad as it is, or as a line of this stroke
down its middle. `Least` (0.7) is the one stated exception to breadth
being data: a ribbon too thin to be seen (its `breadth` is still the
data's, and still the room it takes on its nodes) is drawn as a line of
this stroke, *broader than it is*, and is not to scale. The tree marks
it so, and `Laws.notToScale` lists it.
declarations.title: Ink

modules.comments:
The Sankey engine: the layout this package has had since 0.1, as one
engine among those the renderer draws (`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Engine`).
Pure, so it runs in node.

`Metrics` and `Widths` are this engine's own configuration: `sankey
metrics widths` is the engine, and a `Picture` (words, open groups) is
what it is told as any engine is. It promises `FlowsForward`,
`LayersAligned` and `WidthsConserved` at its own scale; every route it
makes is a `Ribbon`, inked as a `Band` by quantity and as a `Hairline`
in a plain picture. It places no ports: it stacks the edges on a node's
side by where they go, so the edges of one port need not stand
together, and a port would have no one place.

One layout serves both pictures. Every edge has a width, in units; a
node is as tall as the wider of what enters it and what leaves it, and
its edges stack along its sides. A Sankey takes the widths from the
wires' payloads and draws each edge as wide as it is. A plain DAG gives
every edge one unit and draws each as a hairline down the middle of its
place. The positions come from the same code either way: the Sankey
layout in `hylograph-layout`, with its lanes for edges that span more
than one layer. The flow runs left to right (`sankey`), or the way the
engine is told (`sankeyToward`, 0.5).

That layout does the placing (`DataViz.Layout.Sankey.Whole`): the scale
is fixed (`unit` pixels to one unit of width, the layers a fixed
distance apart) and the picture is as large as that makes it; a node no
edge touches stands on a shelf under the picture; and an edge that
closes a cycle, an edge from a node to itself among them, leaves its
source below the edges that go forward, runs back under the picture in a
channel of its own, and enters its target likewise. The engine is the
translation and nothing more: from a projection to rows and names, and
from the layout's boxes and routes to placed nodes and centre lines, set
in from the left by a margin with room for an edge to turn.

## Words, and open groups

Two things the Sankey layout cannot be asked for, and what is done here
about each.

**A node tall enough for its words.** Told what is written in a node
(`words`), the layout wraps it to the node's breadth by an estimate of
each line's width (`Hylograph.Flow.Render.Text`, which says how the
estimate is made and how wrong it can be) and makes the node at least
tall enough for the lines; its edges stand in the middle of its sides.
The breadth is `metrics.nodeBreadth`, one for the picture, so a caller
with long labels may choose narrower and taller nodes.

**An open group, outlined.** Told the grouping and which groups are
closed (what `collapse` was told), the layout gives every open group
that holds a drawn node an outline: a box round its members, with a
strip for its name above them, the outline of a group inside it nested
in it. Nothing that is not a member is inside an outline, and the
outlines of two groups overlap only where one holds the other.

How, in three steps. (1) The Sankey layout runs once, to learn where it
would put everything. From that an order is made: at each level of the
grouping, the groups and the loose nodes by the mean height of what is
in them. (2) It runs again held to that order within every column
(`nodeSort`), so in each column a group's members stand together, the
members of a group inside it together among them, and the groups in the
same order in every column. A long edge's waypoints go with the
innermost group that holds both its ends. (3) `Internal.Bands` then
moves boxes down, never up and never past one another, until every
outline has its padding and its strip and no outline has anything else
in any column it spans; the same pass makes the room a taller node
needs. A member of an open group that no edge touches would be on the
shelf, far from its group: it stands in its group's first column
instead.

What `hylograph-layout` 0.6.0 lacks, exactly, which is why step 3 is
here and not there: a node's height is its value at the scale and
nothing else can be asked (no least height by node); the gap between
two nodes of a column is one number, `nodePadding` (no gap by pair, so
no room for a frame); and a node is in one column (no node that spans
columns, and no notion of a set of nodes to be kept clear of others
across columns). `nodeSort` is the one thing it offers, and it is used.
The cost of doing step 3 afterwards is that the Sankey relaxation does
not know of the moves, so edges into a group that was moved down slant
more than they would if the relaxation had made the room itself.

## Top-down (0.5)

`sankeyToward TopDown` is the same layout stood on end: its layers are
rows, a node is as broad as the broader of what enters and what leaves
it, its edges stack along its top and its bottom, and every edge not
turned back runs down the page. It is made by laying the flow out left
to right and exchanging x and y at the last, so the placing, the order,
the lanes and the channels are the left-to-right layout's, and the laws
it promises are the same three, read by the layout's direction. Four
things do not survive being stood on end, and are done otherwise:

- **A node's words.** Left to right a node is `nodeBreadth` along the
  flow, its words are wrapped to that, and it is made taller where they
  need it. Top-down the words are still wrapped to `nodeBreadth`, which
  is then the most room a node is given across the flow for its words'
  sake: a node is as broad as its ribbons, or as its widest line needs
  where that is more (`Text.breadthOf`), and its ribbons stand in the
  middle of it. So a thin ribbon under a long name has a node as broad
  as the name, and two such nodes cannot have their names collide.
- **How far a node reaches along the flow.** Left to right,
  `nodeBreadth`. Top-down, as tall as the tallest words of any node in
  the picture (one height, so that the nodes of a layer are one row);
  `restHeight` where the picture sets no words.
- **An outline's strip.** An outline's name is in a strip at the top of
  its box, either way. Left to right that is across the flow, and the
  room is made by moving boxes down a column. Top-down it is along the
  flow, before the outline's first row, and the room is in the gap
  between layers (and above the first): for each outline one in another,
  its padding and its strip before, its padding after. Where
  `layerGap` has not room for what the picture asks, the strip and the
  padding are both less, in proportion, and `PlacedOutline.header` says
  what the strip is.
- **The margins.** Left to right the picture has half a `layerGap`
  before its first layer and after its last, room for an edge that turns
  back, whether or not one does (as since 0.1, kept so that no picture
  moves). Top-down it has only what is used: that room where an edge
  does turn back, an outline's where there is an outline, and otherwise
  none, so a picture of forward edges begins at its first row and ends
  at its last, and a page can stand something directly under it.

And one thing is done top-down that is not done left to right: **the
layers are straightened** after room is made. Making room moves boxes
one way only, after the Sankey layout has placed each layer against its
neighbours; so a row of thin ribbons under long names is spread out,
the row they run to is not, and every ribbon between them slants the
same way. Top-down each layer is then moved once more, whole, by the
mean of how far its edges from earlier layers are from straight, each
weighed by its breadth (the layers an outline spans move as one). Left
to right it is left as it was, so that no picture made before 0.5
moves; the header's last paragraph above says what that costs.

The shelf of nodes no edge touches, under the picture left to right, is
at its right top-down.

Signals of identity that do not depend on place (0.6).

When a change of cut moves things (`Continuity` says the pair is only
`Ordered`, or less), another channel has to carry the identity that
position lost. Two are offered to a page as decorations:

- **hue**: a group has a hue, its closed bar is drawn in it, and so are
  its parts when it is open (`hued`). A group inside a hued group that
  has no hue of its own takes the hue of the group over it.
- **the outline bearing the closed name**: the layout engines draw it
  already (`PlacedOutline.name`), for every open group.

The page decides when to use them; `Continuity.continuity` is what it
decides by.

whichever are open; a closed group's step and summary are under the
groups over it and under itself.

declarations.title: hueOf

closed or open, and every edge that leaves such a node likewise (an
edge that leaves a node of no hue takes the hue of the node it enters).

declarations.comments:
The hues of colour by default (0.7): five, in a fixed order.

In a flow drawing any two ribbons may cross, so every *pair* of hues
has to be told apart, not only neighbours. These five are the largest
set found, among the eight hues of a general-purpose categorical
palette and Okabe and Ito's eight, that passes a palette validator on
all pairs, against a white surface: every pair at least 8 apart in
OKLab (times 100) under simulated protanopia and deuteranopia (the
worst is 9.1, yellow and aqua, protan), at least 15 apart in full
colour (the worst 15.6, green and aqua), all in one band of lightness.
Under simulated tritanopia the worst pair is 6.7 apart. No sixth hue of
those tried could be added: so a picture with more than five things to
tell apart reuses a hue, and `Measures.overlapsInOneColour` says where
that matters. (Okabe and Ito's set whole fails the same check on its
yellow's lightness; with its yellow left out its worst pair passes, but
no more than five of it and the other set together pass all pairs.)

Blue, aqua, yellow, green, sky.
declarations.title: palette

declarations.comments:
A colour made lighter (towards 1) or darker (towards -1): mixed with

is itself.
declarations.title: shade

declarations.comments:
Colour by default (0.7): a decoration with every node that gives
anything, and every ribbon, in a hue.

The flow's top-level blocks that give something (a top-level group, or
a node no group holds; one that only receives stays in the ink) take
the `palette`'s hues in the order they are given, round and round. A
group's parts keep the group's hue in shades, from darker to lighter
in the order given, so that two parts of one group can be told apart
and are still seen to be of one group; a closed group's bar is the
group's hue itself. A ribbon takes the colour of where it comes from,
in one of three tints by where it goes (see `tinted` below).
So a ribbon keeps its hue whatever is open, and an overlap is grey on
grey only where two blocks share a hue (more than five give) or two
ribbons leave one node.

`finest`: the flow's projection with nothing closed, in the order the
hues are to be given (the unfolding engine's one order, say: its nodes
sorted by `Unfold.rankOf`). Text is not coloured: the tree writes
every label in the ink.

modules.comments:
Words in a node, set without a DOM.

The layout is pure and runs in node, so it cannot ask a browser how
wide a string is. It estimates. `estimateWidth` adds up an advance for
each character from a table of five classes, in ems, taken from the
metrics of Helvetica and Arial (the same numbers to within a hundredth
of an em): narrow letters and marks a quarter of an em, `f t r` and
brackets a third, `m w M W` near nine tenths, capitals seven tenths,
and everything else (lower case, figures) 0.56. Semibold is taken as
six per cent wider.

HOW WRONG IT CAN BE. For Helvetica, Arial and Liberation Sans the
classes are within about 0.06 em of each glyph's true advance, and over
a label of ordinary words and figures the errors mostly cancel. Measured
once, in Chrome, on 276 lines of cell ranges and short phrases set in
Helvetica Neue: what the browser drew was between 0.87 and 1.01 of the
estimate, 0.97 at the median. So the estimate ran as much as a seventh
too wide (a line wrapped that would have fitted) and a hundredth too
narrow. A face of other proportions is another matter: a condensed face
runs a fifth narrower, a wide one (Verdana) a fifth wider, and the
estimate knows nothing of kerning, letter-spacing or a `text-transform`
set by a stylesheet (upper-casing a label makes it a quarter wider than
estimated). `caution` (1.08 by default) is the factor the estimate is
multiplied by before a line is judged to fit, so that an estimate a
little low still wraps in time; raise it for a wider face. A page can
measure what was drawn (`getComputedTextLength`) against the estimate.

`wrap` breaks at spaces, and inside a word only where the word alone
is wider than the line. Text that would need more than the lines
allowed ends in an ellipsis on the last line.

modules.comments:
A watched change between two cuts: the stages of it, as layouts to be
blended, and a transition of them by the ecosystem's own machinery
(0.6).

When the layouts of two cuts differ, the reader keeps their place by
seeing what moves move. A change is shown in **stages**, so that two
kinds of motion are not on the page at once. Opening a group:

1. **make room**: the closed picture, with every node the change does
   not touch going to where the open picture has it, and the group's
   bar going, whole, to where its parts will stand across the flow
   (nowhere, where they will stand within the span it has);
2. **unfold**: the open picture, with the group's parts starting inside
   the bar (each where it will be across the flow, all where the bar is
   along it) and going out along the flow to their tiers.

Closing is the same two, backwards: fold, then close up. A stage in
which nothing moves is left out. So a pair that is `Held` has no stage
that makes room; and where the group's parts are in one tier it has no
stages at all: the parts take the bar's place at once, and there is
nothing to watch.

Every stage is two layouts of one projection and of one shape
(`Reshape.sameShape`), made with `Reshape.reshaped`, so every picture
part of the way through is `Reshape.blend` of the two, and **conserves
what the two conserve**: a ribbon is as broad as it was and stands
where it stood on its node's side all the way. What a picture part of
the way through does not keep is apartness: in the second stage the
parts start on top of one another, inside the bar.

Between the two stages the picture changes from the closed projection
to the open one. Every untouched node is then in one place in both;
the bar is replaced by its parts, within the span it had; and the
ribbons that met the bar meet the parts, which is the one thing that
is seen to jump (by less than the bar's breadth).

A change that opens some groups and closes others has no stages here:
take it one group at a time. A change with no group opened or closed,
between two layouts of one shape, is one stage.

THE MACHINERY is `hylograph-transitions`: `watched` gives a
`TransitionSpec` of layouts (its engine's, with its easings), whose
tick is pure. Nothing here keeps time, and nothing here runs: a page
runs the spec with that library's own consumer of a transition,
`Hylograph.Transition.Consumers.transitionConsumer` (in
`hylograph-transitions` since 0.1.1), on its `Coordinator`. Until 0.7
this module had a runner of its own, `watch`, because that consumer
lived in `hylograph-simulation`; it is gone, and this package depends
on no simulation.
